findings.title: Static credential grants destructive or outbound capability
findings.detail: 3 tools across 1 server with destructive or outbound capability authenticate with a long-lived static credential.
findings.fix: Move to scoped OAuth where the server supports it, and rotate the key.
findings.remediation: A long-lived API key in an environment variable cannot be scoped per conversation and is not revoked when a session ends. Prefer OAuth with least-privilege scopes, and rotate the key if it has ever been shared.

findings.title: Tool definitions consume a large share of the context window
findings.detail: explicit (no project config) loads 496 tools across 36 servers, using 80.2% of a 200,000-token window before any user input.
findings.fix: Unload servers this project does not use.
findings.remediation: This is spent on every request in the context, before any user input. Remove servers not needed in this project, or split them across projects so each context loads only what it uses.

findings.title: Tool annotations disagree with the tool's name or schema
findings.detail: 1 tool declare a safety annotation that its own name or schema contradicts.
findings.fix: Report it to the server's maintainer; treat the annotation as absent meanwhile.
findings.remediation: A tool declaring readOnlyHint while its name or parameters indicate otherwise is worse than one declaring nothing, because clients and reviewers act on the annotation. Report this to the server's maintainer; until it is fixed, treat the annotation as absent.

findings.title: Tools dispatch on a free-form command, so their real surface is unobserved
findings.detail: 64 of 70 tools on azure take an operation name and a free-form argument object, so what they can do is not in the definition (2 other server(s) too).
findings.fix: Treat a clean drift result for these servers as covering the router, not the operations behind it.
findings.remediation: These tools take an operation name and a free-form object of arguments rather than declaring parameters of their own. What they advertise is a router; the operations it reaches are discovered at call time and never appear in the tool list. Two consequences. Effect classification reads names and schemas, and a router's say nothing, so a tool that creates and deletes is indistinguishable from one that reads. And drift detection compares the advertised surface, so the server can add, remove or repoint any operation behind the router without changing anything this tool can see - a quiet result means the router did not change, not that its capabilities did not. This is usually a token optimisation rather than an attempt to hide, but the property is the same either way: for these servers the definition is not the contract. Pin the version and read the release notes.

findings.title: Tools whose capability could not be determined
findings.detail: 114 tools whose capability could not be determined from name, schema or annotations.
findings.fix: Read what these do before trusting a capability summary that omits them.
findings.remediation: Nothing in these tools' names, schemas or annotations said what they affect, so no class was inferred. They are reported as `unknown` rather than folded into `read`, because absence of evidence is not evidence of harmlessness and the two used to be indistinguishable. A dispatch router is the common case - a tool taking an operation name and a free-form argument object is uninformative by design, and the operations behind it can do anything the server can. Read the documentation for these, and treat any count of destructive tools as a lower bound while they are unresolved.

findings.title: Server version is not pinned, so which build runs is left to chance
findings.detail: 34 local servers run whatever version the package manager had cached.
findings.fix: Pin the version in the config, and re-baseline when you change it.
findings.remediation: A command like `npx -y pkg` does not mean the latest release. The package manager serves a cached copy when it has one, so two machines with identical configuration can run different versions for months, and a version with a known problem keeps running until something clears the cache. Pin the ones you rely on. The version listed below is what each server REPORTS for itself, which is not always its package version: measured across 29 public servers, 16 reported something else, several of them a year stale and one a literal placeholder. Treat it as a claim, not a measurement.

findings.title: Server reports a version that is not the one installed
findings.detail: 16 servers report a version that is not installed on this machine; 9 unrelated servers all report '0.1.0', which is the version of the SDK they are built on rather than their own.
findings.fix: Trust the installed version, not the server's; tell the maintainer.
findings.remediation: The version a server states for itself does not match any copy of its package on this machine. Servers built on the official Python SDK commonly report the SDK's version rather than their own, so several unrelated servers announce the same number. Whatever the cause, the field cannot be used to identify what is running - read the installed version instead, and report the mismatch to whoever maintains the server.

findings.title: Capability profile of the loaded tool surface
findings.detail: In explicit (no project config): 89 can write, 1 can send or reach outside, 75 can do something irreversible; 114 could not be determined.
findings.fix: Check that every destructive and outbound tool needs to be loaded here.
findings.remediation: Review whether every destructive and outbound tool needs to be loaded in this context. Tools the model can see, it can call.
